newsitem.title: EGYPT: Russia warns Israel of renegotiating peace deal.
newsitem.headline: Russia warns Israel of renegotiating peace deal.

text.p: Russia warned Israel on Wednesday that it risked an outburst of violence if it tried to renegotiate peace deals signed with the Arabs.

Russian Foreign Minister Yevgeny Primakov told reporters at this Red Sea resort that Russia -- a co-sponsor of the 1991 Madrid peace summit between Israel and the Arabs -- would make sure both sides adhered to what they agreed upon but with a little help from its regional allies.

"Russia, as a co-sponser of the peace process, thinks the process should end based on the coordinated principles agreed upon... and not from point zero," Primakov said after talks with Egyptian President Hosni Mubarak.
The Madrid peace conference agreed that both Israel and its Arab neighbours would negotiate peace agreements based on the principle of trading Israeli-occupied Arab lands for peace.
"If someone wants to start from scratch, the process will come to a standpoint and the two sides will move far apart from each other, creating an opportunity for violence," Primakov added.
At least 70 people were killed last month in five days of clashes between Israel and the Palestinians sparked by the Jewish state's opening of a tunnel near the holy Moslem al-Aqsa mosque.
For the past three weeks, Israel and the Palestinians have tried to salvage the peace process snagged on a long-delayed Israeli troop withdrawal from the West Bank town of Hebron.

Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, who was elected in May on a platform that refuses handing over occupied Arab lands for peace, is trying to renegotiate the deal to guarantee the security of Jewish settlers living there.

The United States, the other sponsor of the peace talks and Israel's key Western ally, even recalled its special envoy Dennis Ross after he failed to wrangle an agreement but Egypt would not underestimate Russia's contribution.
"She could play a role just to maintain the peace," Mubarak said when asked what Moscow, riddled with its own problems, could possibly do.
"'The divine spirit can empower the weakest of his creatures'," said Moussa, quoting an Egyptian proverb.

"There are common positions among us and Egypt is taking a responsible role... as co-sponsors we like this role and with your help (Russia can help)," said Primakov, in Egypt as part of a Middle East tour to boost Russia's role in the region.
He has already held talks with Syrian and Lebanese leaders and will visit Jordan, Israel and Palestinian self-rule areas.
Europe is also seeking a larger political role to complement its hefty economic contributions to the region and both Egypt and Russia welcomed their involvement.
"We think the European role is very important in support of other roles, the most important being the U.S and Russian roles because they are co-sponsors," Moussa said.

"Their exact role is to be decided by them... but it should be a supportive role in addition to the economic role they already play. The political role is important because it will support the principle of land-for-peace and talks with the Palestinians, Lebanese and the Syrians," he added.
The European Union this week named Spanish diplomat Miguel Angel Moratinos as a special Middle East envoy.
